content.text: Motion is a change in the position of an object with time. Motion occurs throughout the universe: people walk and run, air moves into and out of lungs, blood flows, leaves fall, water flows, vehicles travel, Earth rotates and revolves around the Sun, and the Sun moves within the Milky Way. This chapter describes motion along a straight line, called rectilinear motion. It develops velocity and acceleration, derives equations for uniformly accelerated rectilinear motion, and introduces relative velocity as a way to describe the relative nature of motion. In kinematics, motion is described without investigating its causes; the causes of motion are studied in dynamics.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Introduction and scope of rectilinear motion

content.text: In studying motion, an object may be treated as a point object when its size is much smaller than the distance it travels during a reasonable time interval. In many real-life situations, neglecting the object's size introduces little error. Whether this approximation is appropriate depends on the motion being considered; the chapter's opening discussion uses this approximation for its kinematics treatment.

Average velocity describes how quickly position changes over a finite time interval, but it does not specify the velocity at every instant in that interval. Instantaneous velocity v at time t is the limit of average velocity as the time interval Δt becomes infinitesimally small. It is the rate of change of position with respect to time at that instant. In calculus notation, v = dx/dt. Graphically, instantaneous velocity is the slope of the tangent to the position–time (x–t) graph at the instant considered.

To estimate instantaneous velocity graphically at t = 4 s, draw a secant through points on the position–time curve on either side of that time. With Δt = 2 s centred at 4 s, the secant slope gives average velocity from 3 s to 5 s. Reducing the interval to 1 s gives the average velocity from 3.5 s to 4.5 s. As Δt approaches zero, the secant approaches the tangent at the point and its slope approaches instantaneous velocity. The textbook's example curve is x = 0.08t³; Table 2.1 compares Δx/Δt for successively smaller centred intervals (2.0 s, 1.0 s, 0.5 s, 0.1 s and 0.01 s). The calculated average velocities approach 3.84 m s⁻¹ at t = 4.0 s. When position data or an exact x(t) expression is available, numerical limiting values or differentiation can be used. The printed table was visually inspected; its small entries are not transcribed here individually.
equations: v(4 s) = dx/dt at t = 4 s ≈ 3.84 m s^-1

content.text: Problem: The position of an object moving along the x-axis is x = a + bt², where a = 8.5 m, b = 2.5 m s⁻² and t is measured in seconds. Find its velocity at t = 0 s and t = 2.0 s, and its average velocity between t = 2.0 s and t = 4.0 s. Solution: Differentiate position with respect to time: v = dx/dt = 2bt = 5.0t m s⁻¹. Thus v = 0 m s⁻¹ at t = 0 s and v = 10 m s⁻¹ at t = 2.0 s. Average velocity from 2.0 s to 4.0 s is [x(4.0) − x(2.0)]/(4.0 − 2.0). Since x(4) = a + 16b and x(2) = a + 4b, the result is (12b)/2 = 6b = 15 m s⁻¹. For uniform motion, instantaneous velocity and average velocity are equal at all instants.

content.text: Instantaneous speed is the magnitude of instantaneous velocity. Velocities +24.0 m s⁻¹ and −24.0 m s⁻¹ both correspond to a speed of 24.0 m s⁻¹. Over a finite interval, average speed is total path length divided by elapsed time, while average velocity is displacement divided by elapsed time. Therefore average speed is greater than or equal to the magnitude of average velocity. At an instant, instantaneous speed equals the magnitude of instantaneous velocity.
equations: average speed = total path length / elapsed time

content.text: Velocity can change during motion. Galileo's studies of freely falling objects and objects on inclined planes helped establish that the rate of change of velocity with time is constant for ideal free fall, whereas the change of velocity with distance is not constant and decreases with increasing distance of fall. This led to the concept of acceleration as the rate of change of velocity with time. Acceleration describes change in velocity per unit time.

Average acceleration over a time interval is the change in velocity divided by the elapsed time. Here v₁ and v₂ are velocities at times t₁ and t₂. Its SI unit is m s⁻². On a velocity–time (v–t) graph, average acceleration is the slope of the straight line joining the two corresponding points. Instantaneous acceleration is the limit of average acceleration as Δt tends to zero, a = dv/dt; graphically it is the slope of the tangent to the v–t curve at that instant.
equations: SI unit of acceleration = m s^-2

content.text: Because velocity has magnitude and direction, acceleration may arise from a change in speed, direction, or both. Acceleration may be positive, negative, or zero according to the chosen positive axis. For constant acceleration, a v–t graph is a straight line. The chapter illustrates: (a) motion in the positive direction with positive acceleration; (b) motion in the positive direction with negative acceleration; (c) motion in the negative direction with negative acceleration; and (d) negative acceleration causing an object to move in the positive direction until t₁ and then reverse direction. The sign of acceleration alone does not say whether speed is increasing: speed increases when acceleration and velocity point in the same direction and decreases when they point in opposite directions.

For the position–time graphs described in the chapter, positive acceleration makes the curve bend upward, negative acceleration makes it bend downward, and zero acceleration gives a straight line. Under uniform motion, the x–t graph is a straight line inclined to the time axis and the v–t graph is parallel to the time axis. Under uniform acceleration, the x–t graph is parabolic and the v–t graph is a straight line inclined to the time axis. Some textbook figures contain sharp kinks, which mathematically indicate points where the functions are not differentiable. The text notes that in realistic situations graphs are smooth and velocity and acceleration do not change abruptly at an instant; changes are continuous.

The area under a velocity–time curve between two times represents displacement during that interval. For constant velocity u from t = 0 to t = T, the v–t graph is a horizontal line and the area is a rectangle with height u and base T, so displacement is uT. The dimensions also support this interpretation because velocity multiplied by time has dimensions of length. For uniform acceleration, the area under the straight-line v–t graph is the sum of a triangle and a rectangle, giving displacement x = ½(v − v₀)t + v₀t. The textbook cautions that a fully general proof uses calculus.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Displacement as area under a velocity-time graph

content.text: For motion with constant acceleration, if the initial velocity at t = 0 is v₀ and the velocity at time t is v, acceleration is a = (v − v₀)/t. Rearranging gives v = v₀ + at. This relation connects initial velocity, final velocity, acceleration and elapsed time and is represented by a straight-line velocity–time graph.

For uniformly accelerated motion, displacement equals the area under the velocity–time graph. The area is the sum of a triangle and a rectangle: x = ½(v − v₀)t + v₀t. Since v − v₀ = at, substitution gives x = v₀t + ½at² when the initial position is taken as zero. If the initial position is x₀ instead, the coordinate at time t is x = x₀ + v₀t + ½at².

For constant acceleration, average velocity over the interval is the arithmetic average (v + v₀)/2. Therefore displacement x = [(v + v₀)/2]t. Substituting t = (v − v₀)/a and simplifying gives v² = v₀² + 2ax when the initial position is zero. For nonzero initial coordinate x₀, the general form is v² = v₀² + 2a(x − x₀). This equation connects velocity, acceleration and displacement without explicitly using time.

The chapter derives the constant-acceleration equations by integration. From a = dv/dt, write dv = a dt and integrate from v₀ at time 0 to v at time t, obtaining v − v₀ = at and v = v₀ + at. Next, use v = dx/dt and integrate dx = v dt with v = v₀ + at to obtain x − x₀ = v₀t + ½at². To obtain the velocity-displacement equation, use a = (dv/dt) = (dv/dx)(dx/dt) = v(dv/dx), so v dv = a dx. Integrating gives (v² − v₀²)/2 = a(x − x₀), hence v² = v₀² + 2a(x − x₀). The text notes that the calculus method can also be used for non-uniform acceleration, unlike the constant-acceleration kinematic set in its stated form.

Problem: Obtain the equations of motion for constant acceleration using the method of calculus. The source's solution starts with a = dv/dt, integrates dv = a dt between v₀ and v and 0 and t to obtain v = v₀ + at. It then uses v = dx/dt and integrates dx = v dt, substituting v = v₀ + at, to obtain x − x₀ = v₀t + ½at². Finally it rewrites acceleration as a = v(dv/dx), integrates v dv = a dx, and obtains v² = v₀² + 2a(x − x₀). These results are for constant acceleration in the displayed derivation.

content.text: Problem: A ball is thrown vertically upward with velocity 20 m s⁻¹ from the top of a multistorey building 25.0 m above the ground. Find (a) how high the ball rises above its launch point and (b) how long it takes to hit the ground. Take g = 10 m s⁻². Choose upward as positive. Then v₀ = +20 m s⁻¹ and a = −10 m s⁻². At the highest point v = 0. Using v² = v₀² + 2a(y − y₀), 0 = 20² + 2(−10)(y − y₀), so y − y₀ = 20 m. For the total time, the book gives two methods. Method 1 splits the path: the upward time follows 0 = 20 − 10t₁, giving t₁ = 2 s. From the top, the ball falls from y₀ = 45 m to y = 0 with v₀ = 0 and a = −10 m s⁻², so 0 = 45 − 5t₂² and t₂ = 3 s. Total time is 5 s. Method 2 uses the original launch coordinate y₀ = 25 m, y = 0, v₀ = 20 m s⁻¹ and a = −10 m s⁻² in y = y₀ + v₀t + ½at²: 0 = 25 + 20t − 5t², or 5t² − 20t − 25 = 0; the physically relevant positive time is t = 5 s. The text says the second method is better because constant-acceleration equations do not require splitting the path.

content.text: An object released near Earth's surface accelerates downward under gravity. If air resistance is neglected and the fall height is small compared with Earth's radius, the magnitude g can be treated as constant, approximately 9.8 m s⁻². This is free fall and is a case of uniform acceleration. If upward is chosen as the positive y-direction, gravitational acceleration is a = −g = −9.8 m s⁻². For an object released from rest at y = 0, v₀ = 0, so v = −gt = −9.8t m s⁻¹, y = −½gt² = −4.9t² m, and v² = −2gy when y is the signed coordinate measured from the release point. The source's plotted figures show constant negative acceleration, velocity varying linearly with time, and signed position varying quadratically with time.

Problem: Prove Galileo's law: distances traversed during equal intervals of time by a body falling from rest stand to one another in the ratio of odd numbers beginning with unity, 1:3:5:7:… . Solution in the source: divide the free-fall time into equal intervals τ. Since the object starts from rest, its signed position is y = −½gt². The positions at times 0, τ, 2τ, 3τ, … are found from this relation. Taking y₀ = −½gτ² as the position after the first interval, successive position coordinates are in units proportional to 0, 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, … . Differences between successive positions are therefore proportional to 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, … . Galileo Galilei (1564–1642) established this law and was the first to make quantitative studies of free fall.

content.text: Problem: Derive an expression for the stopping distance of a vehicle in terms of its initial velocity v₀ and braking deceleration. Stopping distance is the distance travelled between applying the brakes and coming to rest. It depends on initial speed and braking capacity. Using v² = v₀² + 2ax and final velocity v = 0, the stopping distance dₛ satisfies 0 = v₀² + 2adₛ, hence dₛ = −v₀²/(2a). Here a is the signed acceleration during braking and is negative if the direction of initial motion is positive; equivalently, if the positive deceleration magnitude is denoted by |a|, dₛ = v₀²/(2|a|). Thus stopping distance is proportional to the square of initial speed: doubling initial speed makes stopping distance four times as large for the same deceleration. The text lists braking distances 10 m, 20 m, 34 m and 50 m at speeds 11, 15, 20 and 25 m s⁻¹ respectively, which it says are nearly consistent with the formula. Stopping distance is important when setting speed limits, including in school zones.
equations: d_s = v0^2/(2|a|) when |a| is the deceleration magnitude

content.text: Reaction time is the time a person takes to observe, think and act. In driving, it is the time between noticing a hazard and applying the brakes. It depends on the complexity of the situation and the individual. The textbook proposes measuring it by asking a friend to drop a ruler vertically through the gap between the thumb and forefinger and measuring the distance d it falls before being caught. The ruler falls under free fall, with v₀ = 0 and a = −g. If the measured distance is d, its magnitude obeys d = ½g tᵣ², so tᵣ = √(2d/g). The source gives d = 21.0 cm and g = 9.8 m s⁻² but the extracted text does not preserve the printed final numerical evaluation clearly; the formula is clear, and the numerical result is not asserted here.

The chapter summary states that an object is in motion if its position changes with time. Position is specified relative to a chosen origin; for straight-line motion, position to the right of the origin is positive and to the left is negative. Average speed is greater than or equal to the magnitude of average velocity over a given interval. Instantaneous velocity is the limit of average velocity as Δt approaches zero, v = dx/dt, and equals the slope of the tangent to the x–t graph at that instant.

Average acceleration is Δv/Δt. Instantaneous acceleration is the limit of average acceleration as Δt approaches zero, a = dv/dt, and is the slope of the tangent to the v–t graph. In uniform motion acceleration is zero, the x–t graph is a straight line inclined to the time axis, and the v–t graph is horizontal. In uniformly accelerated motion, the x–t graph is a parabola and the v–t graph is a straight line inclined to the time axis. The area under a velocity–time curve between t₁ and t₂ equals displacement during that interval.

content.text: For one-dimensional motion with constant acceleration, the kinematic equations relate displacement x, elapsed time t, initial velocity v₀, final velocity v and acceleration a: v = v₀ + at; x = v₀t + ½at²; and v² = v₀² + 2ax when the initial position at t = 0 is zero. If the initial position is x₀, replace x by x − x₀ in the displacement relation and use v² = v₀² + 2a(x − x₀). The equations require constant acceleration and proper algebraic signs for all quantities.

metadata.topic: Chapter summary: kinematic equations and conditions

content.text: The origin and positive direction of an axis are choices that must be stated before assigning signs to displacement, velocity and acceleration. If a particle is speeding up, acceleration is in the direction of velocity; if its speed is decreasing, acceleration is opposite to velocity. This relationship does not depend on the chosen origin or axis. The sign of acceleration itself does depend on the chosen positive direction: with upward chosen positive, gravitational acceleration is negative, yet it increases the speed of a falling object and decreases the speed of an object thrown upward.

content.text: Zero velocity at an instant does not necessarily mean zero acceleration. A particle thrown vertically upward has zero velocity at its highest point but continues to have gravitational acceleration. In the kinematic equations, quantities are algebraic and may be positive or negative; the equations apply to one-dimensional motion with constant acceleration when signs are assigned consistently. The definitions of instantaneous velocity and acceleration are exact generally, whereas the simple kinematic equations apply only when the magnitude and direction of acceleration remain constant throughout the motion.

(a) A railway carriage moving without jerks between two stations. (b) A monkey sitting on top of a man cycling smoothly on a circular track. (c) A spinning cricket ball that turns sharply on hitting the ground. (d) A tumbling beaker that has slipped off the edge of a table.

Choose the correct entries: (a) which child lives closer to school; (b) who starts earlier; (c) who walks faster; (d) whether they reach home at the same or different times; and (e) whether one overtakes the other once or twice. Exercise 2.3 asks the learner to choose suitable scales and plot the x–t graph for a woman who leaves home at 9:00 am, walks at 5 km h⁻¹ to an office 2.5 km away, stays there until 5:00 pm, and returns home by an auto at 25 km h⁻¹. Exercise 2.4 describes a drunkard who takes five 1 m steps forward and three 1 m steps backward, each step taking 1 s, repeating this pattern. It asks for an x–t graph and the time, determined graphically and otherwise, to fall into a pit 13 m from the start. These are exercise prompts; the textbook does not provide worked solutions alongside them.

Exercise question (no solution supplied): A car moving along a straight highway at 126 km h⁻¹ is brought to rest within 200 m. Assuming uniform retardation, find the retardation and the time taken to stop.

Exercise question (no solution supplied): A player throws a ball vertically upward with initial speed 29.4 m s⁻¹. (a) State the direction of acceleration during upward motion. (b) Give velocity and acceleration at the highest point. (c) Choose x = 0 and t = 0 at the highest point, take vertically downward as the positive x-direction, and give signs of position, velocity and acceleration during upward and downward motion. (d) Find the maximum height and the time to return to the player's hands. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance.

Exercise question (no solution supplied): For a particle in one-dimensional motion, state whether each statement is true or false, giving reasons and examples: (a) a particle with zero speed at an instant may have non-zero acceleration at that instant; (b) a particle with zero speed may have non-zero velocity; (c) a particle with constant speed must have zero acceleration; (d) a particle with positive acceleration must be speeding up.

Exercise 2.8 asks for a speed–time graph from t = 0 to 12 s for a ball dropped from 90 m that loses one tenth of its speed at each collision with the floor. Exercise 2.9 asks for clear distinctions, with examples, between (a) the magnitude of displacement and total path length over the same interval, and (b) magnitude of average velocity and average speed. It defines average speed as total path length divided by time and asks the learner to show that the second quantity in each pair is greater than or equal to the first, and to state when equality holds, considering one-dimensional motion. No worked solutions are supplied in the exercise section.
equations: average speed = total path length / time interval

content.text: Exercise question (no solution supplied): A man walks from home to a market 2.5 km away at 5 km h⁻¹. Finding the market closed, he immediately turns and walks home at 7.5 km h⁻¹. Find (a) the magnitude of average velocity and (b) average speed over intervals (i) 0–30 min, (ii) 0–50 min and (iii) 0–40 min. The note emphasizes why average speed is total path length divided by elapsed time, rather than the magnitude of average velocity: the latter can be zero on a completed return journey even though the person has walked a nonzero distance.
equations: average speed = total path length / elapsed time
magnitude of average velocity = |displacement| / elapsed time

The bullet's muzzle speed is 150 m s⁻¹. Find the speed with which the bullet hits the thief's car, choosing the speed relevant for damaging the car. The problem requires distinguishing the bullet's speed relative to the van from its speed relative to the road and from the relative speed between bullet and target.
